correctness.rationale: For a boundary-one pentagon, published Proposition 3.6 identifies the two orientations of each internal diagonal. Substitution into the two oriented local exchange relations gives \(q_{i+1}q_i=1+q_{i+3}=q_iq_{i+1}\), hence adjacent commutativity and a recurrence. Commutativity of \(q_i\) with \(q_{i+4}\), the recurrence \(q_{i+4}=q_{i+1}q_{i+2}-1\), adjacent commutativity, and cancellation by the unit \(q_{i+1}\) force \(q_iq_{i+2}=q_{i+2}q_i\). Distances \(1\) and \(2\) exhaust pairs on five indices. Height \(1\) follows from \(ab=2\) and centrality of \(2\). The published height-\(3\) quaternionic example contains both \(i\) and \(j\), with \(ij=k\) and \(ji=-k\), so it supplies sharpness. No computation is used as proof.

value.rationale: The theorem identifies the exact first height where genuinely noncommuting boundary-one frieze values can occur. It converts the source's separate low-height facts into a uniform structural obstruction over every division ring and is directly useful when classifying or enumerating quaternionic friezes by height. It is not a renaming, numerical recomputation, or arbitrary slice; the pentagon is the natural first unresolved polygon between the published quadrangle classification and the published hexagon example.
